articles.title: The Forest No One Was Meant to See
articles.dek: When Notre-Dame reopened after its fire, the world admired the windows and the bells. The part that actually held the building up was hidden in the rafters the whole time — and Paul says the same is true of the universe you're standing in right now.
articles.quote: Christ doesn't just build the world and step back — he's the hidden beam holding every rafter of it together, right now.
articles.body:
On the night of December 7, 2024, bells that had been silent for five and a half years rang out over the Seine. Notre-Dame de Paris, gutted by fire in 2019, was reopening. Heads of state filled the pews. The choir sang beneath a ceiling that had, not long before, been open to the sky. Cameras lingered on the rose windows, the golden altar, the restored organ's first swelling notes. It was, by any measure, one of the most moving public moments in years — a monument the world thought it might lose, standing again.

But the part of the restoration that mattered most was never on camera. Above the stone vaults, hidden from every visitor who has ever craned their neck to admire the ceiling, sits a lattice of massive oak timbers the French have called la forêt — "the forest" — since the Middle Ages. It is the skeleton that carries the roof. The original forest, built from roughly 1,300 oak trees in the 1200s, burned to ash in an hour. To rebuild it, French foresters and carpenters spent years selecting and hand-hewing more than 2,000 new oak trees, joining the beams the same way medieval builders did — no nails, no steel, just wood fitted into wood. Nobody in the pews that December night could see it. But without it, there is no ceiling, no bells, no rose windows. The whole visible glory rests on an invisible frame.

Paul knew a version of this problem, and he was writing from a jail cell. He had never once visited the church at Colossae. It had been planted by a local believer named Epaphras, who eventually made the long journey to Rome to sit with Paul in his chains and report on how the young congregation was doing. Some of what he described worried Paul deeply: false teachers had moved in, teaching that Jesus was wonderful, sure — but not quite enough on his own. Add a few more spiritual powers to your worship. Observe a few extra rules. Honor a few more unseen forces thought to govern the universe. It was an old temptation wearing new clothes: treat Christ as one impressive support beam among many, rather than the one frame the whole building depends on.

So Paul does something almost startling for a man writing from chains. He doesn't argue point by point. He bursts into praise. In a few sentences he says more about who Jesus actually is than most of us hear in a year of sermons:

The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in him all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. (Colossians 1:15–17, NIV)

Paul isn't finished making his point. A few lines later he adds, "For God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him" (Colossians 1:19, NIV). Not most of God's fullness. Not God's fullness plus a committee of lesser powers to fill in the gaps. All of it. Whatever the false teachers in Colossae thought was missing from Jesus, Paul says, wasn't missing. It was already there, holding everything up, long before anyone thought to ask.

Read that middle line again: in him all things hold together. Not "were held together, once, at the beginning." Present tense. Ongoing. Right now, as you read this sentence, whatever holds atoms to their nuclei and planets to their orbits and your own lungs to the rhythm of breathing is not an impersonal law running quietly on autopilot. Paul says it's a Person. Christ isn't only the architect who drew the plans and walked away. He's the forest in the rafters — the hidden structural reality that everything visible depends on, every single moment, whether anyone notices or not.

Filipino homes have understood a small version of this for generations. The haligi, the main post of a bahay kubo, carries the weight of the whole house, and yet once the roof and walls go up, almost nobody looks at it again. Everyone admires the nipa thatch, the woven walls, the view from the window. Nobody remembers to thank the post. But pull it out, and nothing else stands. Paul is saying Christ is that kind of load-bearing reality for the entire universe — and for your particular week. The same one holding galaxies in their courses is holding your shaky job, your uncertain relationship, the body that isn't cooperating the way it used to. You were never meant to be your own support beam. You were only ever meant to rest on one.

Paul doesn't stop at cosmic architecture, though. He brings it home to something far more personal a few verses later, reminding the Colossians who they used to be:

Once you were alienated from God and were enemies in your minds because of your evil behavior. But now he has reconciled you by Christ's physical body through death to present you holy in his sight, without blemish and free from accusation. (Colossians 1:21–22, NIV)

Notice the movement: once alienated, now reconciled. The same Christ who holds the planets together is the one who reaches down to hold together what sin had pulled apart — your standing with God. That's not a small add-on to a hymn about cosmic supremacy. It's the whole point of it. The one strong enough to sustain a universe is the one gentle enough to mend a person.

Here's the turn worth sitting with: nobody at Notre-Dame's reopening needed to see the forest in the rafters to benefit from it. They just needed to trust the people who built it, and let the building do what buildings do — hold them, quietly, without asking to be thanked. Faith works the same way. You don't have to feel Christ holding your life together to actually be held. The invisible frame doesn't announce itself. It just keeps doing its work, beam by beam, whether you're admiring the windows or not.

Christ doesn't just build the world and step back — he's the hidden beam holding every rafter of it together, right now. That includes your rafters. So today, when something in your life feels like it might come apart at the joints, you don't have to hold it together by sheer will. Look up past the windows you can see, and remember the frame you can't — and rest your weight on it.

articles.title: The Organ That Doesn't Wait for You to Deserve It
articles.dek: A mother, a dying toddler, and a piece of liver that grew back on its own — the body's strangest organ mirrors an invitation God kept making to a people who'd already been sent away.
articles.quote: God didn't wait for Israel to heal itself before inviting them home — he made the healing the reward for returning, not the requirement.
articles.body:
In November 1989, at the University of Chicago Medical Center, a mother named Teresa Smith lay on an operating table beside her twenty-one-month-old daughter, Alyssa. Alyssa's liver was failing from a rare disease, and there was no time left to wait on a donor list. No surgeon in the United States had ever successfully transplanted part of a living adult's liver into a child. So doctors removed a section of Teresa's own liver — about a fifth of it — and placed it inside her daughter, not knowing for certain that either piece would survive the surgery, let alone thrive afterward.

What happened next is the part most people never learn in school. Within about six weeks, Teresa's liver had grown back to nearly its original size. So had the small segment now living inside Alyssa. The liver, alone among the body's major organs, can do this: lose most of its mass — even up to seventy percent of it — and rebuild itself close to full size and function, sometimes within two months. The cells that do the rebuilding, called hepatocytes, normally sit quietly and rarely divide. But injury flips a switch in them, and they start multiplying again almost like the tissue remembers what size it's supposed to be, then stops once it gets there. Ancient Greek storytellers seem to have sensed something true about this organ long before medicine could explain it; in the myth of Prometheus, an eagle devours his liver each day, and each night it grows back whole. The body, it turns out, was quietly built with a stubborn capacity to come back from ruin — no willpower required, no earning it. Just the design, waiting to be triggered.

Jeremiah preached to a nation that badly needed the same kind of news. By chapter 3, the prophet has already laid out, in painful detail, how far Judah had wandered — chasing after foreign gods "on every high hill and under every spreading tree" (Jeremiah 2:20), breaking covenant the way an unfaithful spouse breaks a marriage, sacrificing devotion the family should have kept for one household alone. The northern kingdom, Israel, had gone further still. It had already been sent away — conquered, scattered, divorced, in the very language of chapter 3:8. By any human accounting, that relationship was finished. You don't send a certificate of divorce and then invite the person back into the same house. That's not how betrayal usually gets resolved, not among nations and not around a Filipino dinner table either, where a wounded silence — tampo — can outlast the argument that caused it by years.

Yet that is exactly what God does. "Go, proclaim this message toward the north," he tells Jeremiah. "Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD, I will frown on you no longer, for I am faithful... I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt" (Jeremiah 3:12-13). And then, further on, the line that carries the whole chapter's weight:

"Return, faithless people; I will cure you of backsliding." "Yes, we will come to you, for you are the LORD our God." (Jeremiah 3:22)

Read that order again. God doesn't say, "Heal yourselves, and then come back." He says, come back, and I will do the healing. The cure isn't the condition for the return. The cure is what waits on the other side of it. That's worth sitting with, because most of us assume it works the other way — that we're supposed to arrive presentable, repaired, having already sorted ourselves out, before we're fit to be received. Jeremiah says the opposite. The only thing asked of the faithless people in this whole passage is verse 13's single, small instruction: acknowledge your guilt. Not fix it. Not undo years of damage on your own strength. Just stop pretending it isn't there. A few verses later, in chapter 4, the same invitation gets even more specific: "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, circumcise your hearts" (Jeremiah 4:4) — deal honestly with what's underneath, and let God handle what grows back.

That's exactly how healing works in a living body, too. Teresa Smith's liver didn't regenerate because she trained it to, or earned it through willpower. It regenerated because that capacity was already built into the tissue, waiting to be triggered the moment it was needed. The regrowth wasn't the price of the donation. It was the built-in response to it.

God didn't wait for Israel to heal itself before inviting them home — he made the healing the reward for returning, not the requirement.

It's worth asking where you've quietly assumed the opposite in your own life. Maybe it's the relative you've avoided at every reunion since a falling-out neither side ever named out loud. Maybe it's years of distance from God himself, the kind that builds so slowly you almost don't notice it became a canyon. Maybe it's a marriage or a friendship where both people are waiting for the other to apologize first, each one convinced they need to see repair on the other side before they'll risk the walk back. Filipino families know this particular standoff well — the unspoken rule that someone has to be the one who softens first, and the quiet pride that keeps everyone waiting. Jeremiah 3 suggests a different order entirely: the return comes first. The honesty comes first. The healing — the actual cure for whatever has gone wayward — is what God supplies once you're back in the room, not what you're required to bring with you as an entry fee.

Alyssa Smith grew up healthy. Her mother's liver, and the piece she gave away, both went on doing what livers do — quietly repairing, quietly restoring, long after the surgery made headlines around the world. Jeremiah's message to a scattered, unfaithful nation carries that same quiet confidence: guilt named honestly is not the end of the story. It's the doorway back into a house where the healing was already waiting, prepared before you ever knocked.

So if there's a version of "return" you've been putting off — a phone call, a prayer you've been avoiding, an apology you've rehearsed a hundred times but never said out loud — you don't need to arrive whole. Just arrive. Acknowledge the guilt, however small or large it is. Let the cure be his to give, not yours to manufacture beforehand. That's the invitation Jeremiah carried north almost 2,600 years ago, and it is still standing open today, for anyone who's ever waited too long to go home.

articles.title: The Desert That Learns to Flow
articles.dek: Psalm 107 ends with a strange detail: God doesn't restore his people once and move on. He does it again, every time the ground goes dry.
articles.quote: Restoration isn't a single transaction, it's a rhythm God repeats every time the ground turns dry again.
articles.body:
In the early 1990s, scientists flying over a stretch of northern China looked down on land so eroded that local farmers had a name for it: the yellow earth. The Loess Plateau, an area roughly the size of France, had been stripped of trees, overgrazed, and carved by centuries of rain into a maze of bare gullies. Dust storms rising off it were said to occasionally darken skies as far away as Beijing. Families who scratched out a living on its cracked slopes were among the poorest in the country, and a single hard rainstorm could wash away an entire season's planting in an afternoon. Then, starting in 1994, Chinese officials and international agronomists tried something that sounded almost naive: they cut terraces into the hillsides, planted more than a hundred million trees, and paid farmers to let the worst land simply rest. Skeptics gave it a decade before wind and rain undid the whole project. Instead, within about ten years, satellite photographs showed the plateau turning green. Wheat fields, apple orchards, and grassland now grow where there was once only bare rock and dust. Families who had left for factory work in southern cities came home to farm the same slopes their grandparents had abandoned as hopeless. Conservationists now study it as one of the largest land restorations ever attempted, proof that ground written off as ruined for good can still be brought back to life.

Psalm 107 was written for people who knew exactly what wasted land felt like, and knew that it did not have to stay that way. Much of the psalm is a catalog of rescues: sailors caught in storms, prisoners in chains, wanderers dying of thirst in the desert, all crying out and being saved. But the closing section, verses 33 to 43, does something different. Instead of one rescue story, it steps back and shows the whole pattern, the way God moves through land and lives across years, even generations.

It does not flinch from the hard truth first. "He turned rivers into a desert, flowing springs into thirsty ground, and fruitful land into a salt waste, because of the wickedness of those who lived there" (Ps 107:33-34). Good ground can go to ruin. The psalm says so plainly, without softening it. But barely a breath later, it turns the picture completely around: "He turned the desert into pools of water and the parched ground into flowing springs; there he brought the hungry to live, and they founded a city where they could settle. They sowed fields and planted vineyards that yielded a fruitful harvest; he blessed them, and their numbers greatly increased" (Ps 107:35-38). Wasteland becomes farmland. Hungry wanderers become settled households with vineyards of their own. It is the kind of reversal a Filipino reader will recognize immediately, the same shape as a barangay rebuilding after a typhoon, or a family slowly finding its footing again after years of hardship abroad.

Here is what is easy to miss on a quick read. The story does not end at verse 38. Right after describing this flourishing, the psalm says, "Then their numbers decreased, and they were humbled by oppression, calamity and sorrow" (Ps 107:39). The very people who had just been blessed and multiplied fall into hardship again. That is not a flaw in the poem's logic. It is the point. The psalm is not describing a single rescue. It is describing a rhythm, and the rhythm resolves the same way every time.

"But he lifted the needy out of their affliction and increased their families like flocks." (Psalm 107:41, NIV)

Notice what is not said here. It does not say he lifted them out once, long ago, and left it at that. Read across verses 33 to 41, and God's people go up, down, and up again within the space of a few lines. Fertile land turns to salt waste. Desert turns to flowing spring. Blessing turns to sorrow. Affliction turns, once more, to families increasing like flocks. It is worth asking why a song about God's love would include two full cycles of ruin and restoration in nine short verses instead of just one tidy rescue. The likely answer is mercy, not repetition for its own sake. Restoration isn't a single transaction, it's a rhythm God repeats every time the ground turns dry again.

That is exactly what the farmers on the Loess Plateau discovered. The greening of that land was never a one-time fix. The terraces have to be maintained every season. The young trees still need tending through drought years, and grazing has to be managed carefully so the new grass has a chance to take root. Erosion still threatens the slopes every rainy season, and farmers still walk their fields checking for the first signs of washout. The restoration holds only because someone keeps showing up to keep it holding. It is a picture, in soil and rainfall, of a God who does not restore his people once and move on, but stays close enough to notice exactly when the ground turns dry again.

If there is a wasteland in your life right now, a marriage that feels parched, a body that is tired in a way sleep does not fix, a faith that has gone quiet, this psalm is not promising you that dry season was a one-time mistake you should have avoided. It is older and gentler than that. It is telling you this ground has gone dry before, in other lives, in other centuries, and the same hands that turned that desert into pools of water are not new to this kind of work. They have done it before. They are not tired of doing it again. That has not changed simply because it is your turn to walk through a dry season now.

The psalm ends by naming the response it hopes for, and it is quieter than triumph. "The upright see and rejoice, but all the wicked shut their mouths. Let the one who is wise heed these things and ponder the loving deeds of the LORD" (Ps 107:42-43). The wisdom asked for here is not cleverness. It is attentiveness, the willingness to notice the pattern in your own life the way you would notice green finally returning to bare hills, and to let that noticing turn into gratitude rather than being taken for granted.

Tonight, try naming one place in your life that currently feels like salt waste. Just name it, honestly, to God. It might be small enough to say in a single sentence, or heavy enough that it takes you a while to find the words. Either way, ask him for what the psalm describes: not a single rescue you have to get right the first time, but a pool of water in a dry place, a spring where you expected only thirsty ground. He has turned deserts before. This one is not beyond him either.

articles.title: The City He Chose Not to Take
articles.dek: A Manila driver once had a fortune within reach and no one who would ever know if he kept it — Solomon says what he did next outranks conquering an empire.
articles.quote: The strongest thing a person can conquer is never a city — it's himself.
articles.body:
Manila taxi drivers see everything human beings leave behind — phones, wedding rings, once a bride's veil, forgotten in the rush of a wedding day. But every few years, a story surfaces that stops the whole country for a moment: a driver finds an envelope of cash, or a pouch of jewelry, or once, reportedly, a bag stuffed with a family's entire savings meant for a son's tuition abroad. The passenger is long gone. There's no camera, no witness, no way anyone would ever know. And the driver — instead of driving home richer than he's ever been in his life — pulls over, calls the number on the ID tucked inside, and waits.

It isn't rare enough to be a fluke, and it isn't common enough to be expected. It's rare enough that it makes the news, and common enough that most Filipinos have heard some version of it — the manong who could have kept a fortune and chose instead to hand it back to a stranger who would never have known the difference. Offered a reward afterward, he usually shrugs it off, half-embarrassed to be thanked for something that felt, to him, less like heroism and more like the only decent option on the table. Ask why, and the answer is almost always some version of the same sentence: Hindi po akin 'yan. That's not mine.

Solomon would have recognized that driver instantly — and been more impressed by him than by any king. In his world, the highest measure of greatness a person could achieve was conquest. Assyrian kings carved their triumphs into palace walls; the famous Lachish reliefs, now in the British Museum, show King Sennacherib's army breaching a Judean city stone by stone, boasting in stone about exactly how it was done. A "warrior who takes a city" wasn't a metaphor to Solomon's readers. It was the actual ceiling of human achievement — the thing every ambitious man in the ancient Near East measured his life against. So it's startling that Solomon, writing wisdom for his own son, reaches for a bigger prize than any of it.

"Better a patient person than a warrior, one with self-control than one who takes a city." (Proverbs 16:32, NIV)

Notice what he's not saying. He isn't saying patience is nice, or that self-control is a virtue worth having alongside ambition. He's saying it outranks the single greatest feat a man of his era could accomplish. Taking a city required an army, siege engines, years of planning, and the blessing of fortune. Self-control requires none of that — no soldiers, no walls to breach, no map. It's available to anyone, in any moment, with no equipment but a will surrendered to God. And Solomon ranks it higher than the conquest kings built monuments to.

It's worth asking why. Maybe because taking a city is a war fought against other people, and it's entirely possible to win it and still lose yourself — your integrity, your soul, the kind of man you become in the winning. But the war for self-control is fought against no one but your own appetite, your own anger, your own itch to grab what isn't yours simply because you can. Win that war, and there's no one left to become bitter, resentful, or corrupted by the victory. That taxi driver never fought anyone for that money. He fought himself — and the man who drove home that night was somehow richer for having nothing extra in his pocket at all.

This is where the proverb quietly points past itself, all the way to a greater King. On the night he was arrested, Jesus stood in a garden with twelve legions of angels a single prayer away — enough heavenly force to take not one city but every capital on earth (Matthew 26:53). A sword had already been drawn on his behalf; a man's ear lay bleeding on the ground. Jesus healed the ear, told Peter to put the sword away, and let himself be bound (Luke 22:50-51). He had the power to take the city. He chose instead the patience of the cross — and in doing that, he conquered something no army ever could: sin, and death, and the distance between us and God. The strongest thing a person can conquer is never a city — it's himself. Jesus proved it first, and only afterward asks us to trust him enough to try it.

Most of us will never stand where that driver stood, or where Jesus stood. But we all get smaller versions of the same test, usually more than once a day: the reply we could send that would wound someone back exactly as much as they wounded us. The interruption in a meeting where we could finally say the sharp thing we've been saving. The rumor we could pass along because it's true and it would feel so good to say. Every one of those is a small city, sitting right there for the taking. Proverbs 16:32 says the better prize isn't taking it — it's walking away from it, patient, in one piece, still yourself.

And here's the quiet mercy tucked at the end of this same passage: "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord" (Proverbs 16:33). You don't have to grab the city to secure your future — God is already holding the outcomes you're tempted to seize for yourself. That's what frees a person to put the sword down, to hand back the bag, to let the sharp reply go unsent. Not because the win wouldn't feel good. Because the God who holds every lot in his hand can be trusted with what you didn't take.

So today, watch for your one small city. It might come in traffic, in a group chat, in a decision nobody else would ever know about. When it comes, remember the driver who pulled over instead of driving on, and the King who sheathed the sword instead of calling the angels. Then do the quietly heroic thing: put your hand down, and let God hold what you were tempted to take.
